newsitem.title: USA: EMLICO case to get full hearing in Massachusetts.
newsitem.headline: EMLICO case to get full hearing in Massachusetts.

text.p: A Massachusetts Supreme Court justice has ruled that a dispute between EMLICO and several big reinsurers is serious enough to warrant consideration by a full court rather than a single judge.
Justice John M. Greaney said in a report issued on Thursday that the controversy over EMLICO's 1995 move to Bermuda was "substantial enough to deserve review by the full (supreme) court."
The case has received wide attention because it could affect the degree to which insurers are allowed to restructure themselves in the face of huge environmental claims.
EMLICO, or Electric Mutual Liability Insurance Company Ltd, filed a petition for voluntary winding up shortly after moving to Bermuda from Massachusetts.
EMLICO's sole policyholder was Connecticut-based General Electric Co.
The dispute centers on whether EMLICO acted fraudulently in moving to Bermuda, where liquidation laws are more favorable.
The case pits EMLICO, General Electric, and Massachusetts and Bermuda insurance regulators against reinsurers including Lloyd's of London, Kemper Reinsurance Co. and Hannover Ruckversicherungs AG.

Greaney said the case posed important issues affecting the worldwide insurance industry. "It is fair to say that the losses that have been (and will be) incurred by EMLICO will be staggering, and, correspondingly, the potential liability of the reinsurers, enormous," he wrote.
A lawyer for Kemper Re and Hannover Re cheered the decision to give the case a hearing before the full court.

"We are very pleased that, after months of legal maneuvering by GE and the liquidators of EMLICO, the reinsurers will finally have their day in court on those issues," Joseph McCullough, a lawyer at Lovell White Durrant in Chicago, said on Friday.

But a public relations consultant for General Electric said that EMLICO and GE were still confident of a favorable outcome based on the facts of the case. "This is something we expected," Coleman Nee, of the Boston firm Rasky & Co., told Reuters.
"We felt that the case was going to be heard by a full court eventually anyway," he said.
The Massachusetts insurance commissioner has been asked to submit a brief by July 25, and the reinsurers must submit briefs by August 22.
